subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Valence Bond Theory, Hybridisation, and VSEPR Theory

cards.claim: Four equivalent electron domains directed toward the vertices of a regular tetrahedron correspond to an sp3 hybrid-orbital set comprising exactly four equivalent hybrid orbitals.
cards.quote: In order to explain the characteristic tetrahedral shape of methane (CH4), one 2s and three 2p orbitals of carbon hybridise to form four new equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals directed towards the four corners of a regular tetrahedron.
cards.source: NCERT Class XI Chemistry (Unit 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure), Section 4.4.1 'sp3 hybridisation'
cards.authority: NCERT / IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology

cards.claim: A multiple bond (double or triple bond) counts as a single electron domain around the central atom because the bonding electrons are constrained to the same internuclear coordinate direction.
cards.quote: A double or triple bond is treated as a single super pair or single electron domain because all electrons shared between the two atoms occupy the same region of space between the two nuclei and repel other electron domains as a single unit.
cards.source: Gillespie & Popelier, Chemical Bonding and Molecular Geometry; NCERT Section 4.2 'VSEPR Theory'

cards.claim: Ammonia (NH3) has four electron domains (three N-H single bonds and one central lone pair), producing a tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and a trigonal pyramidal molecular shape with bond angles of approximately 107 degrees due to lone-pair repulsion.
cards.quote: The nitrogen atom in ammonia has four electron pairs: three bond pairs and one lone pair. The electron geometry is tetrahedral, but the repulsion between the lone pair and bonding pairs compresses the H-N-H bond angle to 107° resulting in a trigonal pyramidal molecule.
cards.source: NCERT Class XI Chemistry, Section 4.2; Cotton & Wilkinson, Advanced Inorganic Chemistry

cards.claim: VSEPR predicts electron-pair geometry and relative bond angles from electrostatic repulsion but does not explain orbital wavefunctions, phases, or energetic orbital mixing; Valence Bond Theory accounts for orbital overlap and directional hybridisation.
cards.quote: VSEPR theory gives the geometry of simple molecules but does not explain the nature of chemical bonds or how atomic orbitals overlap. Valence Bond Theory describes bond formation in terms of the overlap of atomic orbitals.
cards.source: NCERT Class XI Chemistry, Section 4.3; Pauling, The Nature of the Chemical Bond

cards.claim: Sigma bonds are formed by end-on (coaxial) overlap along the internuclear axis with cylindrical symmetry; Pi bonds are formed by lateral (side-on) overlap of parallel p orbitals with a nodal plane containing the internuclear axis.
cards.quote: Sigma (σ) bond: This type of covalent bond is formed by the end to end (head-on) overlap of bonding orbitals along the internuclear axis. Pi (π) bond: This type of covalent bond is formed by the lateral or sidewise overlap of atomic orbitals with electron density concentrated above and below the internuclear axis.
cards.source: NCERT Class XI Chemistry, Section 4.3.4 'Types of Overlapping and Nature of Covalent Bonds'; IUPAC Gold Book

cards.claim: Stereochemical wedge-dash notation represents non-coplanar 3D tetrahedral structures using two in-plane solid lines (109.5°), one solid wedge (pointing towards observer), and one dashed wedge (pointing away from observer), distinguishing 3D reality from flat 90° planar Lewis sketches.
cards.quote: In the wedge-and-dash representation, bonds lying in the plane of the paper are shown by normal lines, bonds projecting towards the viewer are shown by solid wedges, and bonds directed away from the viewer are shown by dashed wedges.
cards.source: IUPAC Recommendations on Graphical Representation of Stereochemical Configuration; NCERT Class XI Chemistry Unit 12

cards.claim: In NF3, the steric number and electron-domain count around the central nitrogen atom includes only the 3 N-F bonding domains and the 1 central nitrogen lone pair (total 4 domains); the 9 lone pairs residing on the terminal fluorine atoms do not belong to the central coordination domain.
cards.quote: Only valence electron pairs residing on the central atom (bonding pairs and non-bonding lone pairs) determine the steric number and geometry around that central atom. Peripheral lone pairs on ligand atoms satisfy their own octets and do not alter the central atom's steric domain count.
cards.source: Miessler, Fischer & Tarr, Inorganic Chemistry (5th Ed.), Chapter 3; NCERT Section 4.2

cards.claim: The number of hybrid orbitals produced strictly equals the number of pure atomic orbitals combined: mixing 1s + 2p produces exactly three sp2 hybrid orbitals (120° trigonal planar, as in BF3); mixing 1s + 3p produces four sp3 hybrid orbitals (109.5° tetrahedral, as in CH4).
cards.quote: The number of hybrid orbitals is equal to the number of the atomic orbitals that get hybridised. The hybridised orbitals are always equivalent in energy and shape and directed in space in some preferred direction to have minimum repulsion.
cards.source: NCERT Class XI Chemistry, Section 4.4 'Salient features of hybridisation'; Pauling (1931)
